steps.body: Family claims get one of three verdicts. **Always**: true of every member ("a square is a rectangle"). **Sometimes**: true of some, false of others — proving it takes one example AND one counterexample ("a rectangle is a square": an all-sides-4 rectangle yes, a 5-by-2 no). **Never**: a fact blocks every possible example.

widget.prompt: "A rectangle is a square." Always, sometimes, or never?
widget.counterexample: A 5-by-2 rectangle is not a square.

choices.label: Sometimes
choices.feedback: Right — a rectangle with all sides 4 IS a square (example), and a 5-by-2 rectangle isn't (counterexample).
choices.evidenceText: A 4-by-4 rectangle is a square. A 5-by-2 rectangle is not a square.

choices.label: Always
choices.feedback: The 5-by-2 rectangle is the counterexample — its sides aren't all equal, so it's no square. Some rectangles are, some aren't.
choices.evidenceText: The always claim fails the required example-and-counterexample test.

choices.label: Never
choices.feedback: An all-sides-4 rectangle is both a rectangle AND a square — one example is enough to defeat never.
choices.evidenceText: The never claim fails the required example-and-counterexample test.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Use the family path, fixed triangle givens, or the required example, counterexample, or blocker evidence.
widget.successFeedback: Right — a rectangle with all sides 4 IS a square (example), and a 5-by-2 rectangle isn't (counterexample).

hints: Hunt an example first, then a counterexample.
explanationVariants: One yes (4-4-4-4) and one no (5-2-5-2): sometimes.
Some rectangles are squares; most aren't.
The name's promises settle it — no member can fail.

widget.prompt: "A square is a rhombus." Always, sometimes, or never?
widget.witness: Every square has four equal sides.

choices.label: Always
choices.feedback: Right — every square has 4 equal sides, which is the whole rhombus test. No square can fail it.
choices.evidenceText: Every square has four equal sides.

choices.label: Sometimes
choices.feedback: There's no counterexample to find — equal sides come guaranteed with the square's name. Down the tree, membership is always.
choices.evidenceText: The sometimes claim fails the required no-counterexample test.

choices.label: Never
choices.feedback: Quite the opposite — the square's guaranteed equal sides make it a rhombus every single time.
choices.evidenceText: The never claim fails the required no-counterexample test.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Use the family path, fixed triangle givens, or the required example, counterexample, or blocker evidence.
widget.successFeedback: Right — every square has 4 equal sides, which is the whole rhombus test. No square can fail it.

hints: Is the rhombus test ever failed?

steps.body: **Never** verdicts need a **blocker** — one fact that kills every possible example. "A trapezoid is a parallelogram": never, because ours has exactly one parallel pair and a parallelogram needs two. "An equilateral triangle is a right triangle": never, because equilateral angles are locked at 60° and right demands a 90°. A blocker beats any amount of searching.

explanationVariants: The angle lock is the blocker.

widget.prompt: "An equilateral triangle is a right triangle." Always, sometimes, or never?
widget.blocker: Three 60° angles cannot include a 90° angle.

choices.label: Never — its angles are all 60°, and right needs a 90°
choices.feedback: Right — the 60° lock is the blocker. No example can exist.
choices.evidenceText: Three 60° angles cannot include a 90° angle.

choices.label: Sometimes — if it's drawn large enough
choices.feedback: Size never changes angles — a bigger equilateral triangle still has three 60° corners. The blocker holds at every size.
choices.evidenceText: The sometimes claim fails the required blocker test.

choices.label: Always
choices.feedback: It's the reverse — not only is it not always, no equilateral triangle can EVER have the 90° a right triangle needs.
choices.evidenceText: The always claim fails the required blocker test.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Use the family path, fixed triangle givens, or the required example, counterexample, or blocker evidence.
widget.successFeedback: Right — the 60° lock is the blocker. No example can exist.

hints: What are an equilateral triangle's angles?

widget.prompt: "An isosceles triangle is equilateral." Always, sometimes, or never?

choices.label: Sometimes
choices.feedback: Right — 7, 7, 7 is isosceles AND equilateral (example); 5, 5, 8 is isosceles but not equilateral (counterexample).
choices.evidenceText: 7, 7, 7 is both. 5, 5, 8 is isosceles but not equilateral.

choices.label: Always
choices.feedback: 5, 5, 8 is the counterexample — isosceles by its pair, but the 8 blocks equilateral. Only some isosceles triangles go all the way.
choices.evidenceText: The always claim fails the required example-and-counterexample test.

choices.label: Never
choices.feedback: 7, 7, 7 defeats never — under our at-least-two-equal definition, every equilateral triangle is already isosceles, so examples certainly exist.
choices.evidenceText: The never claim fails the required example-and-counterexample test.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Use the family path, fixed triangle givens, or the required example, counterexample, or blocker evidence.
widget.successFeedback: Right — 7, 7, 7 is isosceles AND equilateral (example); 5, 5, 8 is isosceles but not equilateral (counterexample).

hints: Can you build one of each?
An example and a counterexample: sometimes.
explanationVariants: Up the tree is only sometimes.
Two pairs is never exactly one.
Under our definition, the categories can't overlap.

widget.prompt: Using our definition (exactly one pair of parallel sides): "A parallelogram is a trapezoid." Always, sometimes, or never?
widget.blocker: Two parallel pairs cannot equal exactly one pair.

choices.label: Never — two parallel pairs can't be exactly one
choices.feedback: Right — the definitions conflict head-on, so no parallelogram can ever qualify. That's a blocker.
choices.evidenceText: Two parallel pairs cannot equal exactly one pair.

choices.label: Sometimes — when it has parallel sides
choices.feedback: That's the at-least-one-pair convention, which some books use. Under OUR exactly-one definition, two pairs always disqualify it: never.
choices.evidenceText: The sometimes claim fails the required blocker test.

choices.label: Always
choices.feedback: The reverse — under exactly-one-pair, a parallelogram's second parallel pair disqualifies it every time.
choices.evidenceText: The always claim fails the required blocker test.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Use the family path, fixed triangle givens, or the required example, counterexample, or blocker evidence.
widget.successFeedback: Right — the definitions conflict head-on, so no parallelogram can ever qualify. That's a blocker.

hints: The two branches of the tree can meet.
Which shape is in BOTH the rhombus and rectangle families?
A square says yes; a tilted rhombus says no.
explanationVariants: A square is a rhombus that IS a rectangle; a tilted rhombus is one that isn't — sometimes.
The branches overlap exactly at the squares, so the verdict is sometimes.

widget.prompt: "A rhombus is a rectangle." Always, sometimes, or never?
widget.counterexample: A tilted rhombus has no right angles.

choices.label: Sometimes
choices.feedback: Right — a square is a rhombus that's also a rectangle (example); a tilted rhombus has no right angles (counterexample).
choices.evidenceText: A square is both. A tilted rhombus has no right angles.

choices.label: Never
choices.feedback: The square defeats never — it belongs to BOTH families at once. The two branches meet exactly there.
choices.evidenceText: The never claim fails the required example-and-counterexample test.

choices.label: Always
choices.feedback: A tilted rhombus is the counterexample — equal sides, zero right angles. Only the square-shaped rhombuses are rectangles.
choices.evidenceText: The always claim fails the required example-and-counterexample test.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Use the family path, fixed triangle givens, or the required example, counterexample, or blocker evidence.
widget.successFeedback: Right — a square is a rhombus that's also a rectangle (example); a tilted rhombus has no right angles (counterexample).

takeaways: Always: down the tree, guaranteed by the name's promises.
Sometimes: prove it with one example AND one counterexample.
Never: find the blocker — one fact that kills every example.
steps.teaser: course complete — the coordinate plane mapped and every shape family in its place.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Test a claim by hunting.** Find one example that fits — if none can exist because a fact blocks them, the verdict is never. Find a counterexample too — if you have one of each, it's sometimes. If no counterexample can exist, it's always.

explanationVariants: Every square inherits two parallel pairs, so the verdict is always.
Down the tree — squares can't fail the parallelogram test.

widget.prompt: "A square is a parallelogram." Always, sometimes, or never?
widget.witness: Every square has two parallel pairs.

choices.label: Always
choices.feedback: Right — every square inherits two parallel pairs from its family chain. No counterexample can exist.
choices.evidenceText: Every square has two parallel pairs.

choices.label: Sometimes
choices.feedback: There's no square that fails — the parallel pairs come guaranteed with the name. Down the tree means always.
choices.evidenceText: The sometimes claim fails the required no-counterexample test.

choices.label: Never
choices.feedback: The opposite — every single square passes the parallelogram test by inheritance.
choices.evidenceText: The never claim fails the required no-counterexample test.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Use the family path, fixed triangle givens, or the required example, counterexample, or blocker evidence.
widget.successFeedback: Right — every square inherits two parallel pairs from its family chain. No counterexample can exist.
